text: – Wait, let me tell you about my encounter with Bay Ganyo, Stoicho chimed in.
– Come on, tell it – we all shouted, because we know that Stoycho knows how to tell such c o m e d i e s.

– And this was in Vienna. One morning I was sitting in the café, at Mendlya’s, I had ordered tea and had started to look through our Bulgarian newspapers. I had become absorbed in a very interesting article, which explained the way in which the constitution can be slightly tampered with, even completely dismantled, and yet still remain the untainted one... I was reading like that, carried away; at one point, right over my ear, there came a shout: “O-o-o! Good day!” – and a sweaty hand seized my right hand. I looked up: a broad-shouldered, black-eyed, black-haired and even black-skinned gentleman, with twisted mustaches, with a cheekboned face, with a shaved stubbly beard, dressed (guess in what?) in a frock coat, unbuttoned, under his waistcoat two or three fingers’ width of a red sash, with a white (our kind of white) shirt, without a tie, with a black, tilted cap, with boots and a Vratsa cane under his arm. A young man: at most, at most thirty years old.
– Excuse me, sir – I say to him with humble surprise, – I do not have the pleasure of knowing you.
– What? Don’t you recognize me, you say? Aren’t you Bulgarian?
– I am Bulgarian.
– So?
– So?
– Come on, get up, let’s go for a walk. What are you going to sit here soaking? They call me Ganyo. Get up!
He didn’t need to tell me that he was Ganyo.
– Excuse me, Mr. Ganyo, I am not free now.
– Well then, why are you sitting in the café if you’re not free?
I did not consider it necessary to give him any explanations. But he showed not the slightest desire to leave me alone and kept blurting out to me:
– Get up and take me to the bathhouse. Where is the bathhouse here?

О-ho! To take him to the bath! At first I was a little tempted to lose my temper, but I held myself in check, and not only did I hold myself in check, but I even laughed. It was clear that Bay Ganyo had a real need for a bath: he smelled sour from a distance. There was nothing for me to do. A compatriot — I must serve him. Then I thought to myself, I too will take advantage of the occasion and have a shower. It was hot. We set off and headed for a summer bathing place with a large pool. Along the way, whenever we came across something more noteworthy, I always considered it necessary to point it out and explain it to Bay Ganyo, but I noticed that he listened to me unwillingly and every now and then would casually let slip an indifferent “Oh, is that so?” or “I know,” with which, apparently, he wanted to impress me that he was no fool. Or else he would cut me off with some question, completely inappropriate to what I was explaining to him. I am telling him, for example, something about the monument to Maria Theresa in the square between the Museums, and he pulls me by the sleeve.

– I see, that one over there, with the blue dress, eh? What do you think of her? Come on, tell me, how do you fellows know which one is like that and which one isn’t? I’ve been mistaken many times, eh? – Bay Ganyo adds to his question with a devilish wink.

We arrived at the bathhouse. My heart was tightening—it seemed to sense in advance what was going to happen. We take our tickets at the cashier’s window. Bay Ganyo asks for his “change,” wiggling his fingers as he thrusts them into the little opening. The cashier hands him the remainder with a smile; Bay Ganyo fixes her with oily eyes, takes the money, and expresses his feelings with a peculiar cough. She bursts out laughing; Bay Ganyo, delighted, twirls his left mustache and shakes his head:
– That the frumoza is domnetà. Well now, Stoycho, ask him whether he knows Vlach. -  Știi rumânește? – asks old Bay Ganyo himself.

At that time another visitor came in, and we slipped into the common hall. A circular corridor. Around it, little changing rooms, hidden by curtains. In the middle, a pool, separated from the corridor by a low wooden railing. One goes down into the pool by several small steps. Bay Ganyo and I took two adjoining little rooms. I quickly undressed and went into the cool pool. In the water, a few Germans were dutifully and silently stretching their muscles and puffing. Bay Ganyo delayed for a long time, and behind the curtain of his little room there could be heard groans and the clinking of some glass objects; at last the curtain was drawn back and he appeared in the nude, with hairy chest and legs striped by his socks — holding in his hand a bundle: these were his precious little flasks, tied up in a not very clean handkerchief, which he had been afraid to leave in the little room. “How do you know their walls are sound? They’ll pry off some board, and then go and drown after it.” He looked around at the walls of the corridor, searched for some nail to hang his bundle on; he thinks that if there is a wall, there must also be a nail on it, and he turns to me:
– But these Germans are such simpletons, they don’t have the brains to hammer in even one nail, yet they say that we are the simple ones.

Having finally convinced himself of the Germans’ stupidity, Bay Ganyo hesitantly placed his little cloth with the perfume vials at the entrance of his room, so that they would be before his eyes while he bathed.

– You listen to her, boy – he turned to me, – you bathe yourself, and keep an eye on the flasks too, and watch what I’ll knock together. – And with those words, Bay Ganyo lifted one of his legs and stepped onto the fence... – Just watch...

He stood up, put the other leg in as well, straightened himself, crossed himself, and cried: – Look... Come on, God help me... Hop!... – and hurled himself into the air, twisted his legs into a pretzel, and splash! into the middle of the pool. Jets of water shot up and showered the heads of the Germans, stunned with amazement; rippling circles sprang from the center toward the edges, overflowed behind the pool, sank back again, and when the water, after a few seconds, settled and cleared, everyone in the bath could see Bay Ganyo’s exhausting gesticulations under the water. He rose up, lowered his legs, stepped onto the bottom, stood upright with his eyes closed and his ears plugged, shook the water off himself—puff!—and splashed water through his drooping mustaches—puff!—and squeezed the water out of his hair and face, opened his eyes, looked at me, and laughed:
– Ha, ha, ha... huh? What do you say?...

I was unable to say anything, because he stretched himself out horizontally over the water and began to slap the surface with his hands, started to swim in the “boatman’s” style: splash! — with one hand and kick two strokes backward, splash! with the other hand and another two strokes. The whole pool began to boil. It was as if we were under some waterfall. Waves splashed toward the edges, chains of droplets sprayed all the way to the opposite walls.
– This is what you call “the boatmen’s way” – shouted triumphant Bay Ganyo across the waves; – now wait and let us show them what they call “vampor.”

And, turning onto his back, he began to strike such merciless blows with his feet against the surface of the foaming water that the spray flew all the way up to the ceiling. He quickly rotated his arms to imitate the paddle wheel of the steamer: “Thumpa-lumpa, thumpa-lumpa, fyyyyy,” and Bay Ganyo whistled with his mouth.

The Germans stood petrified in their places. They, in all likelihood, took my companion for some newly arrived Eastern man who had not yet been admitted to the madhouse, and I noticed on their faces not so much indignation as pity. But Bay Ganyo, it seems, read on their faces boundless astonishment at his skill, and so he hurried up the stairs, stood with his legs slightly apart, looked down haughtily at the Germans, began to beat his hairy chest heroically, and cried triumphantly:  
– Bulgarian! Bulgaaar! – and struck his chest even harder.

The proud tone with which he uttered this recommendation said a great deal; that tone seemed to say: “There he is, do you see the Bulgarian! This is he, this is what he is! You have only heard of him, the hero of Slivnitsa, the Balkan genius! Here he is now before you, whole and entire, from head to toe, in the flesh! Do you see what wonders he is capable of performing! And is that all! Oh, what other things he is still capable of! The Bulgarians were simple-minded, eh! Damn those Jews, those Jews!”
– Well then, ask whether there is any soap – said Bay Ganyo to me, after his patriotic enthusiasm had cooled a little, – just look at what my feet have turned into...

And indeed, his feet did not constitute the most suitable model for the Apollo Belvedere. The patterns of his socks had imprinted themselves on his skin—which was already unclean and hairy. As for filth, however, we cannot astonish the Bulgarians: we cannot make even the most fervent imagination picture anything dirtier than what reality itself can present to you...
With these words, Stoycho finished his story.
